actions.body: Autonomous discovery is not merely a function of capability; it is a management problem. Evidence suggests that without intrinsic prioritization, agents default to uniform sampling, which, in high-dimensional or complex sensory environments, is computationally ineffective. Drawing from comparative analysis between biologically constrained systems and freely evolving artificial agents, we find that cognitive cost gradients—limits on memory, energy, and compute—actually facilitate more robust exploration. By imposing depth-oriented search within limited domains, these systems avoid the 'paradox of unconstrained learning.' Intrinsic curiosity appears to be the mechanism by which systems autonomously select these domains, effectively creating their own 'problems' to solve when explicit rewards are absent. Summary: Intelligent systems effectively navigate complex environments by using their own limitations to 'prune' the space of possible actions. Curiosity serves as a survival mechanism that turns a paralyzing sea of infinite possibilities into a tractable set of high-value problems.
actions.lede: Why unconstrained intelligence paradoxically fails to explore, and how intrinsic curiosity serves as a necessary scaffold.
actions.reason: Synthesized project findings provide a coherent narrative suitable for public dissemination on open-ended discovery mechanisms.
actions.title: The Necessity of Constraint in Discovery
